title: Speed, distance and braking
summary: How fast the law allows, how fast is right — and how much distance you need to stop.

lessons.title: Reasonable speed: the duty above every number
lessons.summary: The speed on the sign is an upper limit. The law requires you to drive at a speed that suits the conditions.
lessons.body:
The number on the sign is not an invitation to drive at it. Above every number, the law sets a general duty: to drive at a [[term:reasonable-speed|reasonable speed]].

:::law
You must not drive except at a **reasonable speed** — a speed that takes into account all the circumstances, the road conditions and the traffic on it, and leaves the driver in **full control of the vehicle** (Traffic Regulations, reg. 51).
:::

So you can commit an offence without exceeding the speed limit at all: someone driving at {{fact:speed.urban}} in pouring rain, near a school when it lets out, is driving too fast — even though the sign allows it.

# When you must slow down
The law lists situations where danger is likely, where you must slow down — and stop if needed (reg. 52):
- In a built-up, populated area, and on a stretch of road with houses and pedestrians alongside it
- When the road is not clear
- When visibility is limited, for any reason — fog, rain, glare, darkness
- Before and inside a sharp bend
- Near a group of children or a crowd
- When approaching a [[term:pedestrian-crossing|pedestrian crossing]]
- When approaching the crest of a hill and anywhere your field of view is limited
- On a steep or long downhill stretch
- Before a narrow bridge and while crossing it
- When you meet or overtake a group of people walking on the road, or animals
- Near a bus standing at a stop, and especially near a bus or vehicle carrying children that stops to pick them up or drop them off
- On a [[term:mixed-street|shared street]], in a [[term:traffic-calming-area|traffic-calmed zone]] and in a tunnel

:::tip Rule of thumb
If you are not sure you could stop within the clear stretch of road you can see ahead — you are driving too fast.
:::

# Too slow can be dangerous too
Driving much slower than the flow of traffic creates speed differences, draws overtaking, and surprises drivers behind you. A vehicle forced to drive slowly because of a heavy load or a steep climb must keep to the right, and where the shoulder is paved and clear — drive on the shoulder and let traffic overtake (reg. 48).

:::warn Emergency braking
You must not brake suddenly, except to avoid an accident that cannot be avoided any other way, or for safety reasons (reg. 53). A driver who drives at a reasonable speed and keeps a safe distance almost never needs to brake like that.
:::
keyPoints: The speed limit is an **upper limit**; the duty is to drive at a [[term:reasonable-speed|reasonable speed]] for the conditions.
In rain, in the dark, near children, before a bend, and when approaching a pedestrian crossing — you must slow down.
A slow vehicle keeps to the right and lets traffic overtake it.
Emergency braking is allowed only to avoid an accident or for safety reasons.

lessons.title: The maximum permitted speed
lessons.summary: How fast is allowed on each type of road when there is no sign, and who is more restricted.
lessons.body:
When no sign says otherwise, the maximum speed is set by the **type of road** and the **type of vehicle** (reg. 54). This is a table every driver should know by heart:

| Road type | Maximum speed with no sign |
|---|---|
| [[term:urban-road|Urban road]] | {{fact:speed.urban}} |
| [[term:non-urban-road|Non-urban road]] with no built divider | {{fact:speed.nonurban}} |
| Non-urban road with a built divider | {{fact:speed.nonurban_divided}} |
| [[term:expressway|Expressway]] | {{fact:speed.freeway}} |
| [[term:mixed-street|Shared street]] [[term:traffic-calming-area|and traffic-calmed zone]] | {{fact:speed.traffic_calming}} |

:::remember What counts as a built divider
A barrier, fence or raised traffic island that physically separates the two directions of travel. A painted line on the road **is not** a built divider.
:::

# When there is a sign
[[sign:426]] sets a different maximum speed for a stretch of road — lower or higher than the table. Even a sign has a ceiling: on an urban road it cannot set more than {{fact:speed.sign_cap.urban}}, on a non-urban road with no divider — more than {{fact:speed.sign_cap.nonurban}}, and on an expressway — more than {{fact:speed.sign_cap.freeway}}.

# Vehicles that are more restricted
- **A bus** (not a minibus): up to {{fact:speed.bus.freeway}} on an expressway.
- **A commercial vehicle whose gross vehicle weight is over {{fact:speed.heavy_threshold}}**, a work vehicle and a tour coach: outside the city — even on an expressway — up to {{fact:speed.heavy.nonurban}}.
- **A slow vehicle, a tractor and a mobile machine**: up to {{fact:speed.slow_vehicle}}, and the expressway is closed to them.

:::tech Speed limiter
A bus and a heavy goods vehicle carry a [[term:speed-limiter|speed limiter]] — a device that stops the engine from accelerating past a set speed: {{fact:speed.limiter.bus}} on a bus, {{fact:speed.limiter.truck}} on a heavy goods vehicle.
:::

:::fine
Driving at excessive speed carries a fine and points, scaled to how much you exceeded the limit. Details in the [[chapter:enforcement|Offences, fines and points]] chapter.
:::
keyPoints: With no sign: urban {{fact:speed.urban}}, non-urban {{fact:speed.nonurban}}, with a built divider {{fact:speed.nonurban_divided}}, expressway {{fact:speed.freeway}}.
Sign [[sign:426|icon]] overrides the table, within the ceiling the law allows.
A commercial vehicle over {{fact:speed.heavy_threshold}} — up to {{fact:speed.heavy.nonurban}} outside the city.

lessons.title: Reaction distance, braking distance and stopping distance
lessons.summary: From the moment you see danger until the vehicle stops — two stages, and both get longer with speed.
lessons.body:
When danger appears, the vehicle does not stop on the spot. The distance it travels until it stops — the [[term:stopping-distance|stopping distance]] — has two parts:

1. **[[term:reaction-distance|Reaction distance]]** — the distance the vehicle travels from the moment the danger appears until the foot presses the brake pedal. During this time the vehicle keeps travelling at full speed.
2. **[[term:braking-distance|Braking distance]]** — the distance the vehicle travels from the start of braking until it stops.

**Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance**

[[widget:stopping-distance speed=90 reaction=1]]

# Reaction distance
An alert driver's [[term:reaction-time|reaction time]] is about one second: to notice, understand, decide and move the foot. Reaction distance = speed × reaction time, so it **grows in direct proportion to speed**: at 90 km/h the vehicle travels 25 metres every second.

Reaction time gets longer — sometimes double or more — when the driver is tired, distracted (a phone!), has drunk alcohol, or has taken medication that affects alertness.

# Braking distance
Braking distance **grows with the square of the speed**: double the speed — quadruple the braking distance. It also depends on:
- **The road surface** — braking distance on a wet road is far longer than on a dry one, and on gravel, mud, oil or ice it is longer still.
- **Tyre condition** — a worn tyre struggles to clear water and grip the road.
- **Brake condition** and vehicle weight — a heavy, loaded vehicle needs more distance.
- **Gradient** — going downhill, the vehicle stops over a longer distance.

:::tech What ABS does
The [[term:abs|ABS]] system stops the wheels from locking under hard braking, so the driver can keep steering and go around an obstacle while braking. It does **not** necessarily shorten the braking distance. In an emergency stop in a vehicle with ABS, press hard and do not ease off — you will feel the pedal pulse; that is normal.
:::

:::remember
Someone who doubles their speed from 50 to 100 km/h doubles their reaction distance — and their braking distance grows fourfold.
:::
keyPoints: Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance.
Reaction distance grows in direct proportion to speed; braking distance grows with the square of the speed.
Fatigue, distraction and alcohol lengthen reaction time.
A wet road, worn tyres and heavy weight lengthen braking distance.
ABS keeps your ability to steer while braking; in an emergency stop, press hard and do not ease off.

lessons.title: Keeping distance from the vehicle ahead
lessons.summary: The gap is measured in seconds, not metres — that way it adjusts itself to your speed.
lessons.body:
Most rear-end accidents happen because the driver did not have enough time to react. That is why the gap from the vehicle ahead is measured in **time**: how many seconds will pass until you reach the point where the vehicle ahead of you is now.

:::law
You must keep a gap that lets you stop at any time and avoid an accident, taking into account speed, road conditions, visibility and traffic. In any case, behind a vehicle in the same lane the gap must not be smaller than **{{fact:following.min_time_gap}}** (reg. 49).
:::

One second is the **minimum the law allows**, not a safe gap. The recommendation is to keep at least **{{fact:following.recommended_gap}}**, and more in difficult conditions.

[[widget:following-distance speed=90]]

# How to measure it
1. Pick a fixed landmark at the side of the road: a pole, a sign, a bridge's shadow.
2. When the back of the vehicle ahead passes it, count: "one thousand and one, one thousand and two."
3. If you reach the point before you finish counting — you are too close. Slow down a little and check again.

# When to increase the gap
- In rain, and especially in the season's **first rain**, when the road is especially slippery
- In fog, in the dark and in glare
- Behind a motorcycle — it can stop in a very short distance
- Behind a heavy vehicle that blocks your view of the road ahead
- When driving a loaded vehicle or towing
- When someone is tailgating you: a large gap ahead lets you brake gently, so they also have time to react

:::tip
When a vehicle merges into the gap you left — do not get angry and do not close up. Just slow down a little until the gap returns.
:::
keyPoints: The gap is measured in seconds; the legal minimum is {{fact:following.min_time_gap}}.
It's recommended to keep at least {{fact:following.recommended_gap}}, and more in rain, in the dark, and behind a motorcycle or a heavy vehicle.
Measure it using a fixed landmark and counting: "one thousand and one, one thousand and two."

lessons.title: Speed and impact force
lessons.summary: Why every extra km/h changes so much in a crash.
lessons.body:
A moving vehicle carries [[term:kinetic-energy|kinetic energy]]. In a crash, all that energy is released at once — crushing metal, breaking bones. And the energy grows with the **square of the speed**: double the speed — four times the energy.

[[widget:speed-energy speed=50]]

A way to feel this: hitting a fixed obstacle at 50 km/h is equivalent to falling from a height of about 10 metres — roughly the third floor. At 100 km/h — a fall from about 40 metres.

# Pedestrians and riders
[[term:vulnerable-road-user|Vulnerable road users]] — pedestrians, cyclists and motorcyclists — have no frame, seatbelt or airbag. A pedestrian's chance of surviving being hit by a vehicle drops sharply as the impact speed rises: at 30 km/h most of those hit survive, and at higher speeds the risk of death rises several times over. This is why the maximum speed in traffic-calmed zones and shared streets is {{fact:speed.traffic_calming}}.

:::remember
A difference of 10 km/h before a pedestrian crossing can be the difference between a vehicle that stops before the child and one that hits them — because while the slower vehicle has already stopped, the faster one is still moving.
:::
keyPoints: Kinetic energy grows with the square of the speed.
A crash at 50 km/h is equivalent to a fall from the third floor.
In areas with pedestrians, low speed saves lives.
